title: Artificial Intelligence and High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Analysts
pub: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper Series No. 20-84 / SSRN working paper 3681574
author: Jillian Grennan · Roni Michaely

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source accepts the distinction between improved output and worker welfare, adding micro-level evidence that AI can simultaneously improve work product, displace high-skilled analysts and redirect workers toward harder-to-replicate soft skills. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution against inferring aggregate employment effects from occupational moves.
qs: We provide detailed micro-level evidence of high-skilled workers job displacement, improved output, and a shift by the labor-force to using alternative skills that are harder to replicate by technology.

While we cannot speak to aggregate employment changes from technological pass-through effects (Aghion et al., 2020) or sectoral shifts (Bena and Simintzi, 2018; Zator, 2020), we do document that analysts leave for non-research jobs.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core task-reconfiguration account and materially extends it with task-level evidence from another high-skilled profession: AI exposure simultaneously displaced some analysts, improved forecast quality and redirected remaining work toward social and complex tasks. Its sector-specific microdata also reinforces the cluster’s caution against inferring aggregate professional displacement, though it does not address legal verification or apprenticeship risks.
qs: We provide detailed micro-level evidence of high-skilled workers job displacement, improved output, and a shift by the labor-force to using alternative skills that are harder to replicate by technology.

While we cannot speak to aggregate employment changes from technological pass-through effects (Aghion et al., 2020) or sectoral shifts (Bena and Simintzi, 2018; Zator, 2020), we do document that analysts leave for non-research jobs.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s task-level redesign thesis with empirical evidence from another high-skilled profession: AI substitutes for easier analytical work while redirecting remaining professionals toward complex, qualitative and interpersonal tasks. It materially extends the synthesis by documenting simultaneous occupational exits, improved forecast performance and declining research novelty, although it does not address legal verification or operating-model requirements.
qs: The key takeaways of our paper is that the relation between AI and the future of high- skilled work is likely to involve some direct substitution but also greater incentives for ana- lysts to use their soft skills – ones that cannot be automated – to engage with management and clients and to develop more complex investment ideas.

The tests suggest that AI serves as a replacement for easier prediction problems, but this then frees up time for employees to work on other tasks such as such as gathering soft information or selling research.

st.t: Assisted performance: Gains vary by skill measure
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious, outcome-specific interpretation. Its coefficients vary materially across specifications, while missing dependent-variable labels, instrument details and truncated results prevent treating them as uniform performance gains or strong causal evidence.

st.t: Junior hiring: Stable unemployment can hide adjustment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account of partial job transformation and expertise complementarity: it interprets AI as shifting high-skilled workers toward social and cognitively complex tasks, while emphasizing that limited short-term skill development may constrain both adjustment and productivity gains. It does not directly address unemployment or junior hiring.
qs: In conclusion, our findings are broadly consistent with the notion that a key consequence of AI will be to shift high-skilled workers toward tasks that rely on social skills and complex thought.

This suggests that an important factor in how much AI will disrupt high-skilled work, and ultimately improve labor force productivity, is the extent to which high-skilled workers can be encouraged to invest in enhancing social skills.

kp.k: Analyst evidence supports both substitution and task complementarity
kp.d: This 2020 working paper studies sell-side security analysts, not legal services. Its task-based framework distinguishes displacement of prediction work from reallocation toward complementary tasks. The authors find evidence of both: more exposed analysts leave sell-side research or change coverage, while remaining analysts increasingly undertake social and complex informational tasks. These are findings within financial analysis rather than direct findings about lawyers.
qs: If analysts only task is prediction, the framework suggests that AI directly substitutes for analysts resulting in job loss.
If analysts’ jobs consist of multiple tasks, then this framework suggests that removing the prediction task from analysts’ jobs allows them to focus their attention on complementary tasks.

kp.k: Exposure measures data-driven competition rather than internal adoption
kp.d: The main sample covers 2010Q1–2016Q4; Table II reports 73,778 analyst-quarter observations and 5,938 unique analysts in its first specification. AI intensity is the number of stock-related social media posts obtained from TipRanks, whose Smart Score generates investment ratings from eight factors. Portfolio exposure is the proportion of stocks in the highest quartile of social media coverage. The authors argue that external AI competition matters even when analysts or their employers do not use AI themselves.
qs: Due to the merging of various datasets, our main sample period runs from 2010Q1 to 2016Q4.
AI intensity is the number of social media posts discussing stock i in quarter t which we obtain from TipRanks.

Thus, even if analysts do not pay attention to social media or even if analysts’ firms do not use AI tools, they will feel competitive pressure from AI because it will be harder for them to bring value to their clients through the traditional means of selling research reports that contain novel trading angles.

kp.k: Causal interpretation depends on a headline-length instrument
kp.d: To address nonrandom stock portfolios, the authors instrument exposure using below-median USA Today headline lengths, aggregated across covered stocks where appropriate. They argue that advertising-related space constraints create quasi-random headline length and that shorter headlines encourage social media posting. They report strong first stages, headline-content checks, microcap placebo tests and plausibly exogenous sensitivity estimates. Their causal interpretation remains conditional on the exclusion restriction; instrument relevance alone does not establish that assumption. Table B.3 also reports small, statistically significant negative coefficients for earnings events, while earnings-surprise coefficients are insignificant.
qs: Our IV is an indicator for a stock having headline lengths below the median headline length in the USA Today in a given quarter.

If the assumption that headline length is uncorrelated with other drivers of analysts’ career decisions, stock coverage, and reporting quality is valid, conditional on controls, then the IV strategy generates a consistent estimate.

Specifically, we document that for a subset of microcap stocks where we expect short headlines to have no first stage effect on AI intensity, the short headline instrument also has no reduced form effect on initiating or ending stock coverage.

kp.k: Higher exposure predicts departures, especially among accurate analysts
kp.d: The authors interpret a one-standard-deviation increase in portfolio exposure as approximately 2.4 additional high-AI stocks and an approximately 0.6-percentage-point increase in departures, about 15% above a 3.9% quarterly baseline. They report an approximately 60% relative increase for highly accurate analysts, but the supplied text inconsistently gives that outcome’s baseline as 0.7% in the introduction and Table I versus 0.073% in the results discussion. The outcome combines departure and prior top-quartile accuracy across the analyst sample, rather than directly measuring a conditional quit rate among accurate analysts. All-star departures show no statistically significant association. Departure is operationalized as disappearance from IBES, not necessarily unemployment.
qs: The baseline quit rate is 3.9% per analyst-quarter, suggesting a 15% increase over the baseline.
In contrast to accurate analysts, we cannot reject the null hypothesis that AI intensity is not associated with All-star analysts quitting and leaving the profession.

Analyst Leaves and Is in Top 25% of Accuracy is an indicator variable for if analyst j stops appearing in the IBES dataset altogether and was in the top 25% of accuracy across all analysts in quarter t − 1.

kp.k: Departures increasingly lead to non-research work
kp.d: LinkedIn and internet career histories indicate an increasing shift toward non-research jobs, including investor relations, other finance roles, consulting and strategy. Table B.5 describes 398 departing analysts between 2004 and 2016; the exposure-based IV destination regressions use 209 observations. Table IV associates greater prior exposure with more non-research employment at the 5% significance level and less research employment at the 10% level, with no significant FinTech effect. Thus, the table qualifies the narrative statement that both destination effects meet the 5% threshold.
qs: We see a significant increase in analysts going to non-research jobs and a significant decrease in analysts going to research jobs.
We observe no statistical difference in their propensity to go to FinTechs.

This result is consistent with the competitive pressure from AI making it harder for analysts to bring value to their clients through better research, and thereby, incentivizing these analysts to pursue careers that does not compete with AI.

kp.k: Remaining analysts shift coverage away from high-exposure stocks
kp.d: The IV estimates associate a one-standard-deviation increase in stock-level AI intensity with a 0.043-standard-deviation reduction in initiating coverage and a 0.018-standard-deviation increase in ending coverage under analyst fixed effects. The authors translate these into approximately 1.9 and 0.5 percentage points respectively, or 7% below and 10% above baseline rates. Stock-fixed-effect estimates are larger. Table V’s OLS ending-coverage estimates are negative whereas the IV estimates are positive, qualifying the narrative description of qualitative similarity.
qs: Thus, when a stock moves into the upper quartile of social media coverage, an analyst decreases his likelihood of initiating coverage on that stock by 1.9% in a given quarter, or about 7% below the baseline rate.
Column 3 of Panel B shows that a one standard deviation increase in AI intensity is associated with a 0.018 standard deviation increase in ending coverage of that stock.

Given that again we see larger economic magnitudes with the alternative fixed effects, we take the estimates that control for some time-invariant unobserved factor about the analyst to be our most conservative estimates.

kp.k: Task reallocation favors complex questions and interpersonal work
kp.d: Earnings-call estimates show more questions and greater question complexity with higher exposure. Complexity is proxied by word count, and topic classifications use selected keywords rather than direct measures of conceptual difficulty. The authors report fewer easy-to-measure questions and more hard-to-measure questions, although the latter relationship is significant only at 10% in the within-stock specification and insignificant without stock fixed effects. Main meeting estimates imply approximately 2.7 additional quarterly meetings. However, Table B.6’s analyst-fixed-effect estimates show increased investor meetings, decreased management meetings and no significant increase in total meetings, qualifying a uniform within-person expansion of interpersonal activity.
qs: Specifically, we find that analysts ask more questions and the complexity of their questions increases when AI intensity is higher.
Question Complexity on Earnings Call is the average total word count in the questions asked by analysts based on Capital IQ transcript data.
Our sample statistics show that, on average, about 85% of these meetings are with management.
In Appendix Table B6, we report the results with analyst fixed effects which suggest that analysts focus relatively more on marketing their research to investors.

kp.k: Forecast improvements coexist with heterogeneity and composition effects
kp.d: Within analyst-stock pairs, the authors find improved accuracy and bolder forecasts, interpreting boldness as a proxy for effort. Bias reductions and aggregate accuracy improvements vary in statistical significance across normalizations; Table X reports a significant reduction in consensus forecast error. Alternative analyst-by-year specifications associate exposure with lower accuracy across covered stocks. Improvements are concentrated among historically accurate analysts, who also leave more frequently, while the lowest accuracy quantile shows deterioration. The authors therefore distinguish improvements within continuing relationships from changes caused by coverage and workforce composition.
qs: The final column of Table IX helps inform if analysts are exerting more effort. It presents evidence that suggests analysts are generating bolder forecasts.
In contrast to the previous results, when we allow for heterogeneity in the stocks analysts cover, we find reporting quality declines in relation to AI intensity.
Importantly, in Panel C, we evaluate consensus forecast error, and find that analysts’ consensus forecast improves.

kp.k: Lower compensation is inferred, not directly observed
kp.d: The authors use market responses to recommendation revisions as indirect evidence about research value and compensation. Table XI covers 39,454 recommendations; OLS estimates associate greater AI intensity with excess-return responses lower by approximately 24–27 basis points across the reported event windows and reduced excess trading volume. The authors interpret these results as diminished research novelty and likely lower compensation, despite better forecasts. The paper does not directly observe pay or independently measure novelty.
qs: While there is no publicly available data set on analysts’ compensation, we know their compensation is linked to abnormal trading volume generated by their research and to the overall value of their research (Brown et al., 2015).
The evidence suggests that the market is less responsive to analyst recommendations when AI intensity is high.
In conclusion, we find indirect evidence to suggest that analysts’ compensation is decreasing.

kp.k: Social-skill investment is a conditional workforce recommendation
kp.d: The authors conclude that adaptation may depend on encouraging high-skilled workers to strengthen social skills and complex thought, while acknowledging that these skills are difficult to improve quickly. This is a forward-looking implication rather than an evaluated training intervention. They explicitly cannot establish aggregate employment effects from technological pass-through or sectoral shifts. The paper also discloses that data supplier TipRanks is a company in which Roni Michaely holds stock and serves on the board.
qs: While those skills are certainly essential, they are often hard to improve in the short-term.

This suggests that an important factor in how much AI will disrupt high-skilled work, and ultimately improve labor force productivity, is the extent to which high-skilled workers can be encouraged to invest in enhancing social skills.

While we cannot speak to aggregate employment changes from technological pass-through effects (Aghion et al., 2020) or sectoral shifts (Bena and Simintzi, 2018; Zator, 2020), we do document that analysts leave for non-research jobs.
Some of the data used in this study comes from TipRanks, a firm in which Roni Michaely has an stock interest and serves on the Board of Directors.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Grennan and Michaely claim that AI both substitutes for sell-side analysts’ prediction work and complements their social and complex-information tasks.
pts.d: In this finance-domain source, the authors report that greater AI exposure increases departures from sell-side analysis, especially departures involving highly accurate analysts, and redirects remaining analysts toward lower-AI stocks. They estimate that a one-standard-deviation increase in portfolio AI intensity raises departures by approximately 0.6 percentage points against a 3.9% quarterly baseline, or about 15%. They report approximately 60% higher departures involving highly accurate analysts relative to baseline, although the introduction and results section give inconsistent absolute baseline figures. The departure indicator for accurate analysts combines departure with prior top-quartile accuracy; it is not simply a quit rate estimated only within that subgroup. Institutional Investor All-star departures show no significant association. Higher exposure also corresponds to ending stock coverage about 10% more often and initiating coverage about 7% less often than baseline. The authors interpret more complex earnings-call questions, a shift toward harder-to-measure topics, and increased meetings as complementary task reallocation. They report improved forecast accuracy, reduced bias, bolder forecasts and improved consensus forecasts, alongside reduced market responsiveness to recommendations, which they interpret as lower research novelty and indirect evidence of lower compensation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on observational panel data and instrumental-variable estimates; task allocation, effort and compensation are partly inferred from proxies.
pts.d: The authors combine IBES analyst records, stock and financial data, Capital IQ events and earnings-call transcripts, TipRanks social-media data, and LinkedIn career histories. The main career regressions contain 73,778 analyst-quarter observations and 5,938 unique analysts; the next-job IV analysis uses 209 observations. AI intensity measures stock-linked social-media posts, rather than directly measuring AI adoption or predictive performance; high intensity denotes the top quartile. Their instrument is below-median USA Today headline length, attributed to editorial space constraints and expected to increase social-media attention. They report first-stage tests, headline-content and firm-characteristic checks, alternative specifications, placebo tests and plausibly exogenous bounds. Causal interpretation depends on the exclusion restriction. Question complexity is proxied by word count, topics by keywords, social-skill activity by event counts and effort by forecast boldness. Compensation is not directly observed: OLS market-reaction estimates show approximately 24–27 basis points lower excess returns per standard-deviation increase in AI intensity, with reduced trading-volume responses. The authors disclose Michaely’s stock interest and board membership in TipRanks.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The empirical claims concern 2010–2016 predictive AI in financial analysis; broader future disruption is conditional and has no specified deadline.
pts.d: The working paper is dated August 26, 2020. Its main sample covers 2010Q1–2016Q4, with career-trend comparisons extending back to 2004. It concerns AI-generated investment recommendations and earnings prediction, not contemporary generative legal AI. The authors’ task-based interpretation distinguishes substitution for prediction from complementarity where workers can reallocate effort toward interpersonal and complex-information tasks. They suggest that future disruption and productivity gains depend on workers’ ability to improve social skills. Empirical qualifications include specification-dependent meeting and quality results: analyst fixed effects yield more investor meetings, fewer management meetings and no significant increase in total meetings; analyst-by-year specifications show declining accuracy across covered stocks, whereas within-pair estimates support improvement. Some bias and topic coefficients are not statistically significant. The authors do not claim to establish aggregate employment effects.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are sell-side analysts, their brokerage employers, corporate management and investment clients; no legal-sector effects are directly studied.
pts.d: Analysts covering portfolios with more high-AI stocks face greater competitive pressure, shifts in coverage and tasks, and increased exits. Historically accurate analysts are disproportionately implicated in departures and in forecast-quality improvements; All-star reputation does not show the same departure association. Departing high-exposure analysts are more likely to move into non-research work such as investor relations, finance, consulting or strategy, with no significant difference in FinTech destinations. Remaining analysts increasingly engage in client communication and complex information gathering. Corporate management and institutional investors are counterparties in these interactions, and investment clients receive the resulting forecasts and recommendations. Brokerage employers may face reduced research-related trading responses, while compensation consequences remain inferred. The authors argue that competitive exposure can arise from external AI providers even when analysts or their employers do not use AI themselves. Their broader relevance claim concerns high-skilled information suppliers, not demonstrated effects on lawyers.
